---
title: "Methods"
subtitle: "How beta(t) is estimated, validated, and turned into cfs"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("_common.R")
```

## 1. The response comes from the null IPM

Recruitment is `log(recruits / spawner)`, taken from the posterior of the
**flow-naive** integrated population model, with a recruit lag from spawning to
the age at which fish are counted.

That "flow-naive" is not a detail. Using the flow-informed IPM's abundances as
the response would put flow on both sides of the regression: the response would
already contain the flow effect the regression is trying to estimate, and the
result would be biased toward finding one. Survival is modelled on the logit
scale, because a multiplier on a probability is meaningless at 0.95 and trivial
at 0.05.

```{r resp-set}
if (is.null(RESP)) NA_("the response has not been built", "R/01_build_response.R") else
  TBL(data.frame(Setting = c("recruit lag (years)", "stock node", "sites built"),
                 Value = c(as.character(RESP$rec_lag %||% "?"),
                           RESP$stock_node %||% "?",
                           paste(names(RESP$sites), collapse = ", "))),
      caption = "As built.")
```

Two lags are easy to confuse and they mean different things. The **recruit lag**
is biology: fish counted at age 2-3 were spawned three years earlier, so they
pair with that year's stock. The **flow lag** is statistics: which calendar
year's hydrograph the IPM's own model selection chose. When the flow lag equals
the recruit lag, the mechanism sits in the spawning year - adult access, redd
site selection, incubation. One less, and it sits in the age-0 rearing year -
emergence timing, displacement, first-summer rearing. Different hypotheses, and
a wrong value shifts everything by a year while still producing a plausible
curve.

## 2. Standardizing the hydrograph

Three steps, in this order, and the order matters.

1. **Logs.** Discharge is multiplicative; 50 cfs means something different in
   April and September.
2. **Subtract the day's mean across years.** Now a positive value means "wetter
   than this date usually is", not "it is June". Without this, beta(t) spends
   itself fighting the seasonal cycle, which dwarfs any anomaly.
3. **Divide by one global standard deviation** - not by each day's own. Per-day
   standardization would make a 2% wobble in a stable January week and a doubling
   in June both equal "one SD", erasing exactly the difference beta(t) is meant
   to weigh.

The geometric-mean discharge on each day, `Qbar(t)`, is kept, because it is the
bridge from beta(t) to cfs (section 5).

## 3. Estimating beta(t)

365 unknown coefficients from roughly 40 years cannot be fitted directly. The
hydrographs themselves supply the constraint: they are smooth and highly
autocorrelated, so a handful of **modes of variation** describe nearly all of
how years differ. beta(t) is estimated inside the span of those modes and rotated
back onto the day axis.

```{r fpc}
if (is.null(BR)) NA_("beta(t) has not been fitted", "R/03_fit_beta_recruitment.R") else {
  k <- BR$k_beta
  cat(sprintf("Components retained: %s.\n\n",
              if (is.null(k)) "see fpc_modes.csv" else paste(k, collapse = ", ")))
  f <- file.path(TAB, "fpc_modes.csv")
  if (file.exists(f)) TBL(utils::read.csv(f), caption = "Retained flow modes and the variance each explains.")
}
```

**The objection, stated plainly.** The modes are ranked by variance in the
*predictor*, without reference to the response. A low-variance flow mode that
carries the real biological signal is discarded before it is ever tested - the
standard critique of principal-component regression (Jolliffe 1982, *Applied
Statistics* 31:300-303). beta(t) cannot show structure the retained modes cannot
build. Changing the retention threshold swaps one arbitrary number for another;
it does not answer the objection, and it belongs in the paper rather than a
footnote.

## 4. The gate

beta(t) always comes out of the arithmetic. The gate decides whether it means
anything, and it is the most important output in the project.

```{r gate-all}
if (is.null(GATE)) NA_("validation has not been run", "R/05_validate.R") else
  TBL(GATE[grepl("^beta", GATE$form),
           intersect(c("site","process","form","n_years","edf","r2_insample",
                       "r2_loo","r2_blocked","p_value","finest_p","passes"), names(GATE))],
      caption = "Every site and process. r2_blocked and p_value are the two that decide.")
```

**`r2_insample`** is optimistic by construction: the model has seen these years
and spent `edf` degrees of freedom on about forty of them. Context only.

**`r2_loo` versus `r2_blocked`.** Leave-one-out leaves a held-out year's
immediate neighbours in the training set, and both hydrographs and responses are
autocorrelated between adjacent years, so the model can half-recognize the test
year from its neighbours. The gap between the two is that leak, made visible.
Blocked cross-validation holds out contiguous runs of years instead, and
**can be negative** - meaning worse than predicting the long-run mean, which is
the honest verdict when a model has learned noise. That is why the threshold is
"greater than zero" rather than something comfortable.

**`p_value`** comes from permuting the alignment between response and flow while
preserving each series' own autocorrelation. The null is not "flow is noise"; it
is "this response, paired with the wrong years of this flow record". Its smallest
attainable value is `finest_p`. A p equal to that floor means no permutation
matched the true alignment, not that p is precisely that number.

Both conditions must hold. Where two estimator arms were run, agreement between
them is a further requirement: if they disagree, the daily structure is coming
from the estimator rather than the data, and no daily recommendation is
defensible.

## 5. From beta(t) to cfs

beta(t) is per standard deviation of log anomaly. A manager releases cfs. Adding
`dQ` on day *t* changes the standardized anomaly by `log(1 + dQ/Q)/sigma`, so at
that day's baseline discharge the benefit per cfs is approximately

$$ \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial Q}(t) \;\approx\; \frac{\beta(t)}{\sigma\,\bar{Q}(t)} $$

Because discharge spans more than an order of magnitude across the year,
dividing by `Qbar(t)` **reshapes** the curve. The best day to release water is
often not the day with the largest beta(t), and half the management answer lives
in that division.

## 6. The two Reclamation questions

**One year at a time (script 08).** Each scenario-year's hydrograph is scored
with beta(t), standardized against the *training* climatology - never against the
scenario's own, which would re-centre a uniformly drier future to look average
and make the effect vanish. The day-by-day attribution then separates two cases a
single number cannot: flow dropping on days that matter, and flow dropping a lot
on days that do not.

**Sustained, at equilibrium (script 10).** The same forecasts held indefinitely,
propagated through the population model to equilibrium abundance and maximum
surplus production. It can point the other way from the annual view, because
equilibrium compounds.

```{r bor-caveat, results='asis'}
cat("\n> The current exports build each future period by shifting the 1950-1999\n",
    "> sequence forward by 45, 75 and 105 years. Every 29 February then lands on\n",
    "> 28 February of a non-leap year and collides with it, and the reverse case\n",
    "> empties 29 February in the target leap years. Both are handled explicitly.\n",
    "> A consequence for interpretation: all three periods share one historical\n",
    "> weather sequence, so the across-year spread within a scenario is that\n",
    "> record's own variability and the period contrasts are paired by construction.\n\n", sep = "")
```

## 7. What this does not establish

The gate tests prediction, not causation. A validated beta(t) predicts years the
model has not seen; it does not identify the mechanism, say whether the relation
holds outside the observed flow range, or confirm that the retained modes were
the right ones. Flow recommendations ultimately rest on mechanism, and this
analysis constrains it rather than supplying it.
